Volume 15 · Chapter 07

Economic history and historical inference

Advanced Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v15-c06

By the endUse historical evidence to distinguish mechanisms and avoid anachronistic causal claims.

Capability and prerequisites

Use historical evidence to distinguish mechanisms and avoid anachronistic causal claims. Prerequisite: political economy and institutions, price indices, present values, causal inference and Bayesian comparison. The task is to connect a documented past to a precisely limited conclusion. Every numerical case below is synthetic: its numbers are teaching inputs, not reconstructed observations of Britain or any former colony.

The past does not arrive as a clean dataset

Suppose an archive shows higher wages after a factory opened, a border separates two institutional histories, and a bank survived after emergency lending. Each observation suggests a question. None, alone, establishes an improvement in household welfare, a causal institutional effect or the necessity of a rescue. Records were made for particular administrative purposes; survivors may differ from missing units; choices responded to information available at the time. A historical explanation must account for those features rather than attaching a modern regression to an inherited table.

Economic history combines chronology, accounting, mechanisms and counterfactual comparison. Chronology establishes what could precede what. Accounting prevents a story from spending the same resources twice. A model identifies which constraints and incentives could produce the pattern. Comparative evidence asks whether the pattern discriminates among explanations. A convincing study needs these parts to agree, while allowing some questions to remain unidentified.

Separate an actor's information set from the historian's. An investment that failed after an unexpected war may have been reasonable beforehand; a successful gamble need not have been prudent. Likewise, do not describe an institution as effective simply because it survived. Survival can reflect coercion, exclusion or benefits to decision-makers rather than broad prosperity. Causal explanation and moral evaluation answer different questions, and neither erases the other.

1. Reconstruct the object before estimating its change

A usable historical observation needs its original document identifier, date of event and recording, geographic unit, unit of account, population covered and transcription rule. Preserve the original string alongside any standardized value. A fiscal year is not automatically a calendar year; a posted wage is not annual earnings; a tax assessment is not a market sale; a modern boundary may divide an older district. A name match is a probabilistic linkage decision, not an identity supplied by spelling alone.

Build a source-to-variable table. For each derived series record the source vintage, conversions, missing observations, interpolations and revisions. An interpolation can help display a trend but cannot create independent observations for standard errors. If a currency changed definition, convert according to a documented rule and preserve uncertainty. Do not treat a blank as zero without evidence that the recorder used blanks that way. Compare scans or double-entry transcriptions for a sample of difficult entries and record disagreements.

The Bank of England research-data catalogue describes very long coverage for selected UK variables and occasional early benchmarks, rather than a uniform annual panel of every modern aggregate. Its version3.1 is described as updated through2016. This is a route to historical evidence, not a claim that the current page supplies a continuous medieval national-accounts dataset or that this chapter has verified its workbook.

Worked case 1 — a wage increase with changing prices, workdays and coverage

Consider two synthetic dates, early and late. A comparable job pays daily cash wages10 and15; paid days are200 and160. Two goods have price vectors p0=(1,2), p1=(2,2), in cash per physical unit. Reference baskets are q0=(2,1) and q1=(1,2). The primitive record is (w0,w1,d0,d1,p0a,p0b,p1a,p1b,q0a,q0b,q1a,q1b)=(10,15,200,160,1,2,2,2,2,1,1,2).

The early-basket price index is L=(p1·q0)/(p0·q0)=6/4=3/2. The late-basket index is P=(p1·q1)/(p0·q1)=6/5. Daily real-wage ratios are(15/10)/L=1 and(15/10)/P=5/4. Annual cash earnings grow only from2000 to2400, so their corresponding real ratios are4/5 and1. Thus (L,P,dailyL,dailyP,annualL,annualP)=(3/2,6/5,1,5/4,4/5,1). The same nominal daily increase supports different precise purchasing-power statements depending on basket and workdays.

These baskets are declared measuring rods, not proven utility-maximizing choices. Consequently L and P are not automatically upper and lower bounds on one household's true cost-of-living index. Such a claim needs stable preferences and revealed-preference conditions, and a welfare comparison also needs hours, household size, noncash compensation, leisure, health and public goods. A numerical index cannot silently supply those assumptions.

Now a separate archive contains late annual earnings for80 of a known100workers, with observed mean2400. Suppose the20missing outcomes are only known to lie in the closed interval[0,3000]. The full-population mean is .8·2400+.2·m, where m is their mean, giving the sharp bounds (lower,upper)=(1920,2520). Assigning all missing workers zero or3000 attains the endpoints. Intermediate real-valued earnings can attain every interior mean. This does not authorize treating missing people as average observed earners; nor does the first representative worker's wage path become a population estimate.

2. Industrialization: distinguish invention, adoption and diffusion

Industrialization is a joint question about methods of production, the scale and organization of activity, sectoral employment, energy, markets and living conditions. A machine can increase output per worker in one task without immediately raising economy-wide output per person. Its sector may be small, complementary transport or skills may be absent, or capital and labor may be absorbed in transition. Conversely, a modest initial productivity effect can enable later expansion. Specify the margin and horizon before calling a change revolutionary.

Allen’s2011article offers a factor-price account of British invention and subsequent diffusion: expensive labor and inexpensive energy can make a labor-saving technique especially attractive, while later improvements widen where it pays to adopt. This is an attributed historical hypothesis. Demonstrating that a technique would be profitable at some measured prices does not establish that these prices caused its discovery, that they were themselves exogenous, or that knowledge, institutions and trade were unimportant.

An adoption calculation is a conditional cost comparison. An invention explanation additionally requires the cost and probability of discovery, access to skills, appropriability of returns and the number of potential users. An explanation of diffusion needs transport, installation, repair, credit, complementary inputs and the feasible techniques available at each date. Present-day engineering knowledge must not be placed in the historical choice set before it existed.

Worked case 2 — profitable in one place, then profitable elsewhere

One unit of output can be made with old inputs10labor-days and1energy-unit. A new technique uses4labor-days and5energy-units plus a rental charge12. Labor costs w per day, energy costs e per unit; output quality is identical, all input markets can supply these quantities, and there are no omitted installation or financing constraints. Costs are C0=10w+e and C1=4w+5e+12. The saving is S=6w−4e−12. These are one-period costs;12 is a rental or annualized charge, not an undiscounted investment treated as an annual bill.

At locationH with (w,e)=(4,1), costs are41 and33, saving8. At locationL with(2,2), costs are22 and30, saving−8. The exhaustive two-technique comparison selects the new method at H and the old at L. In general adoption is weakly profitable exactly when w≥(2/3)e+2, with indifference on the boundary. The checked inputs and outputs are (oldL,oldE,newL,newE,rental,wH,eH,wL,eL)=(10,1,4,5,12,4,1,2,2) and (oldH,newH,savingH,oldL,newL,savingL)=(41,33,8,22,30,-8).

Suppose discovery costs80 up front in the same one-period present-value units, will succeed with certainty and serve20identicalH users. A licensing institution lets the inventor capture half each user's saving, leaving adoption privately worthwhile. Receipts are20·8/2=80: discovery just breaks even. At10users receipts40 fail to cover80. The same adoption advantage can therefore coexist with no private invention. This reduced example assumes the financing of80 is available; it does not infer financing merely from a positive eventual payoff.

Later, a refined technique becomes available with3labor-days,3energy-units and rental8. AtL it costs6+6+8=20, saving2 against the old method. The earlier nonadoption and later adoption are both cost minimizing with the knowledge and prices at their respective dates. The result does not imply that L's earlier producers were irrational. Nor does a high wage alone prove universal advantage: higher energy requirements and capital charges matter separately.

3. Historical institutions and natural experiments

A historical discontinuity is useful only if it creates a defensible comparison. Draw the boundary or intervention timeline using contemporaneous rules before looking at outcomes. Ask whether the border followed earlier prosperity, geography, military strength or settlement; whether people moved across it; whether enforcement matched formal assignment; and whether records were made comparably on both sides. “Long ago” does not mean randomly assigned. Control variables measured after an institution changed may be mediators rather than legitimate confounders.

The Acemoglu–Johnson–Robinson study proposes a chain from settler mortality through colonial institutions to later income. Albouy’s critique challenges data comparability and assignments; the authors’ reply disputes exclusions and coding choices and defends robustness. These linked abstracts establish the existence and broad content of the methodological dispute, not its resolution. A serious extension must audit the underlying records and competing specifications. An instrumental-variable estimate is not made credible by choosing the preferred conclusion before doing that work.

Persistence itself is not a unique mechanism. A historic institution may leave legal rules, roads, schooling, settlement patterns or distributions of political power. If a historical instrument changes several of these channels, the exclusion restriction for a single present-day institutional index can fail. One may identify a bundled historical treatment while failing to identify the independent effect of one component. State which effect the design could recover.

Worked case 3 — a border comparison with bounded departures

Two synthetic districts have outcome means at dates−2,−1,+1: treatedT=(4,5,9), comparison C=(3,4,6). A historical rule starts between−1 and+1; units are a comparable outcome index, not actual national GDP. The pre-period change difference is(5−4)−(4−3)=0. The post difference-in-differences is D=(9−5)−(6−4)=2. With no anticipation, stable composition, no spillovers and parallel untreated changes after−1, D identifies the treated district's effect. Equal observed prechanges are compatible with that assumption but do not prove the unobserved post-period counterfactual.

Let δ be the treated-minus-comparison untreated change, and let s be a positive policy spillover on C. Then D=τ+δ−s, so the treated effect is τ=D−δ+s. If δ∈[−1/2,1/2] and s∈[0,1], unrestricted jointly within that rectangle, the sharp range is[3/2,7/2]. Each endpoint follows from an allowed corner; the affine map attains every value between. These are sensitivity restrictions supplied by the analyst, not confidence intervals learned from the six means. The markers are (Tminus2,Tminus1,Tplus1,Cminus2,Cminus1,Cplus1)=(4,5,9,3,4,6) and (pre,D,lower,upper)=(0,2,3/2,7/2).

For a separate synthetic IV design, let Z be a binary historical instrument, X an institutional score, and Y an outcome. Suppose the mean difference in X by Z is−3/10 and the reduced-form difference in Y is−3/5. Under the structural relation Y=βX+γZ+u with E[u|Z=1]=E[u|Z=0], β=(−3/5−γ)/(−3/10). Exclusionγ=0 givesβ=2. Allow γ∈[−3/20,3/20]; the positive derivative−1/(−3/10) makes the range (excluded,lower,upper)=(2,3/2,5/2). This constant-effect illustration is not automatically a LATE model. If the first stage approaches zero, the same exclusion uncertainty yields a much wider range; a precise historical narrative cannot repair a weak numerical denominator.

4. Crises: reconstruct the balance sheet and the decision date

Anson and coauthors’2017archival study studies the Bank of England's1847,1857and1866crisis transactions using archival lending and refusal records. Its findings distinguish variation in lending practice across episodes, rather than assuming one timeless operating rule. The paper's discussion also distinguishes a later summary of Bagehot's approach from the original wording. Those are reasons to consult transaction records and institutional context before treating a historical slogan as a complete decision procedure.

Three questions must be separated. Did an institution lack cash at the moment creditors demanded payment? Did its assets cover its promised obligations at defensible holding values? What would happen to other institutions and taxpayers under intervention or nonintervention? Liquidity support can address the first without resolving the second; the third requires a wider counterfactual. A ledger of successful borrowers omits applicants refused and institutions that never applied. Low realized losses among recipients can reflect good screening, favorable shocks or support itself; it does not prove the same lending would have been safe to everyone.

Use contemporaneous information when evaluating a decision, then distinguish later evidence about its consequences. Do not place a later central-bank mandate, deposit guarantee or accounting rule into an earlier institution without documenting that authority. A balance-sheet analogy can clarify mechanics while leaving monetary regimes, ownership, collateral law and political constraints different.

Worked case 4 — liquidity finance is not recapitalization

A synthetic intermediary has cash20, loans with face120, and deposits100. Loans pay .9 per unit of face at a final date with certainty; cash and deposits carry no interest. Before a run, holding-value equity is20+108−100=28. Early withdrawals of60 exceed cash by40. The loan-sale market is stipulated to absorb any required quantity at .8 per face unit. Selling50face raises40, leaving70face to pay63, against remaining deposits40. Final equity is23. The five-unit loss equals50(.9−.8); this is a transfer to outside buyers under the stipulated fixed fundamentals, not demonstrated destruction of five units of aggregate output.

Instead, an emergency lender can advance40 at gross repayment1.05. Cash20plus the advance meets withdrawals60; all120face loans remain and pay108. After remaining deposits40 and emergency repayment42, equity is26. A pledge of50face is worth45 at the stipulated certain payoff, covering42. Thus (cash,face,recovery,deposits,withdrawal,saleprice,loanrate)=(20,120,9/10,100,60,4/5,21/20) and (initialequity,soldface,saleequity,loanrepayment,loanequity,collateralpayoff)=(28,50,23,42,26,45). Lending improves this intermediary's equity relative to the sale, but the interest2 goes to the lender, and the five-unit sale discount would benefit buyers. A social intervention claim needs effects beyond this distributional accounting.

If recovery is instead .6, initial equity is20+72−100=−8. The same hypothetical advance would leave72−40−42=−10 after withdrawals and repayment. Pledged50face pays only30, failing the earlier coverage test. The original lending facility cannot simply apply unchanged: the new borrower is insolvent and does not meet its security condition. If a public guarantee nonetheless permits the advance, someone must absorb the shortfall; a transfer of10at the final date restores zero equity under the stipulated payment priority. Its payer must be included. Calling that transfer liquidity does not remove its fiscal incidence.

5. Comparative inference: ask what each explanation predicts

Comparative history benefits from a mechanism table rather than a list of similarities. State an explanation, the sequence it predicts, what records would be expected if it were true and a rival that could produce the same endpoint. Seek evidence at the points where predictions differ. The relevant absence is an observation that would probably have been recorded and preserved under the mechanism; absence from an incomplete archive is weaker evidence.

Select comparison cases using a defensible population or a declared theoretical contrast. Choosing only industrial successes makes failure of the proposed sufficient conditions invisible. Choosing only crises hides the normal periods needed to understand risk. A small set of cases can illuminate implementation and timing without estimating a population frequency. Where numerical likelihoods cannot be defended, report qualitative discrimination and uncertainty rather than inventing posterior precision.

Worked case 5 — three citations can contain only two observations

Use two deliberately simplified, mutually exclusive candidate explanations H1 and H2, with equal prior probabilities conditional on this two-model list. Let E be a newly discovered input-cost record and L be a later adoption-timing record. Stipulate Pr(E|H1)=4/5, Pr(E|H2)=2/5, Pr(L|E,H1)=3/4 and Pr(L|E,H2)=1/4. Their joint likelihoods are3/5and1/10. Posterior odds are prior odds1times likelihood ratio6, giving Pr(H1|E,L)=6/7. The conditional probabilities explicitly handle the sequence; independence has not been assumed.

A second book repeats the same originalE record. It is a citation toE, not a new draw ofE. Counting it again multiplies odds by2and gives the unjustified12/13. If the timing record were instead equally likely conditional on E under both models, say1/2, it would add no discrimination and the posterior would stay2/3. The input/output checks are (prior,EgivenH1,EgivenH2,LgivenEH1,LgivenEH2)=(1/2,4/5,2/5,3/4,1/4) and (joint1,joint2,correct,duplicated,nondiscriminating)=(3/5,1/10,6/7,12/13,2/3).

This calculation teaches source dependence, not a numerical verdict on the Industrial Revolution. Actual explanations such as factor prices and institutions can operate together. If the two-model list omits their combination or another mechanism, a high conditional posterior does not show that H1 is a complete or true account. Discovery and preservation also affect the likelihood of seeing E and L: one must model the observation process or restrict the conclusion to the selected records. The same distinction applies when several historical datasets inherit one original transcription.

A defensible historical research package

Start with an explicit unit, period and estimand. Produce a dated narrative of feasible choices and information, a document inventory with archive identifiers, a variable dictionary and a transparent transcription/cleaning log. Keep uncertain readings and linkages inspectable. State which observations are original, reconstructed, imputed or absent. Link each factual sentence to evidence of the appropriate scope; a later commentator is evidence of that commentator's account unless the underlying event is separately supported.

Then supply the accounting or behavioral model, a comparison design and its assumptions, negative or contradictory evidence, alternative codings and sensitivity ranges. Reconstruct definitions across changing boundaries and report what happens without disputed observations. Compare both micro records and independent aggregates where possible. A broad national series and a local ledger can disagree because they measure different populations, not because one must be fraudulent.

Finally, separate what is established, what remains conditional and what would change the interpretation. A valid conclusion may be narrower than the motivating question. An institution's local effect under a particular historical constraint does not determine the effect of copying its formal name elsewhere. The achievement is a credible explanation with visible limits, not a universal lesson extracted from a memorable episode.

Exercises

  1. In case1 late paid days are180rather than160. Compute annual earnings and both real annual ratios. Explain why neither establishes a population welfare gain.
  2. Of100workers,60are observed with mean2400and40are missing with earnings in[1000,3000]. Derive sharp population-mean bounds. Give a completion attaining each and explain why replacing missing earnings by2400is an assumption.
  3. In case2 use w=3,e=2with the original new technique. Determine the global choice, the exact break-even wage and whether w=10/3is a unique adoption choice. Then compute the refined technique's cost and saving at L.
  4. Assume a risk-neutral inventor maximizing expected profit. Keep H's saving8, discovery cost80and inventor capture share1/2. Find the smallest integer number ofH users making certain discovery weakly worthwhile. Repeat if discovery succeeds with probability1/2, produces no revenue on failure and the cost80is certain. Identify a financing assumption.
  5. Recompute the case3 treated-effect bounds if untreated change difference is in[0,1] and spillover in[0,1/2]. Show endpoints and explain why zero pretrend difference does not narrow this rectangle by itself.
  6. In the separate IV illustration keep reduced form−3/5and direct-effect bound[−3/20,3/20], but change first stage to−1/10. Derive the effect interval and its width. What fails if the first stage is zero?
  7. For the solvent bank in case4, the fire-sale price is now3/4. Compute face sold, remaining loan payoff and final equity. Find the largest gross emergency-loan rate for which borrowing40weakly beats this sale, then impose the same50face collateral coverage rule. Identify the feasible rate bound.
  8. For recovery .6, explain why the original lending rule fails. Under the expressly changed arrangement that a guarantee permits the40advance at1.05and a final transfer covers all obligations, calculate the required transfer and compare it with initial insolvency. Consolidate the lender's interest receipt and payer's transfer; do not call every bank loss a social resource loss.
  9. In case5 use prior Pr(H1)=1/4. Calculate the correct posterior and the posterior if the E record is counted twice. Explain how two authors copying one ledger differ from two genuinely conditionally independent observations.
  10. Design a historical study of whether a new railway raised district prosperity. Specify dates and feasible information, units and records, route selection, population/boundary changes, a comparison and interference problem, two rival mechanisms, and a result that would weaken your preferred explanation. Give an honest scope for the conclusion without inventing observations.
Full solutions and evaluation criteria
  1. Late earnings are15·180=2700, versus2000early. The nominal ratio is27/20; dividing by3/2gives9/10and by6/5gives9/8. Thus (earnings,earlybasket,latebasket)=(2700,9/10,9/8). These are different basket-based measures for the stipulated job, not a common utility index. Population composition, unpaid time, other household earnings and health remain unmeasured. One cannot choose the favorable basket after seeing the result and call it a welfare finding.
  2. The mean is .6·2400+.4·m, so (lower,upper)=(1840,2640). Give every missing worker1000or3000respectively to attain the endpoints. Constant missing earnings between those values attain every intermediate mean. A strong design fixes a district geography or documents a crosswalk, separates announcement, construction and opening dates, and specifies whether prosperity means real earnings, output per resident or another outcome. Record who generated wage, freight, tax and population data and how coverage changed. Explain route selection using plans and contemporaneous constraints; anticipated growth can attract railways, so a simple before/after comparison is insufficient. A comparison district must have a plausible untreated trajectory, while network access and redirected trade may contaminate it. Rival mechanisms might be lower transport costs versus selective migration of skilled workers, or market access versus a simultaneous public investment. Examine freight prices, firm entry and composition as mechanism evidence without conditioning away the total effect mechanically. A prior upward divergence, prosperity gains preceding a credible announcement, or gains explained entirely by boundary reclassification would weaken a causal interpretation. Full credit requires all requested design components, a falsifiable rival comparison and explicit limits; no single railway episode establishes a universal return to infrastructure.

Teach-back

Explain to a historian why a valid cost comparison need not establish the cause of invention, and to an economist why a carefully estimated coefficient can fail when the underlying record changes meaning.

Answer guide

Adoption conditions take the technique as available; invention requires a discovery process, expected market, skills, funding and rewards. A coefficient compares coded observations, so changing population coverage, units or administrative incentives can change the variable without changing the intended economic object. Documentation and model-based inference complement each other.

Delayed retention

After a week, reconstruct the difference between daily and annual real earnings; write the adoption threshold; deriveτ=D−δ+s; explain liquidity versus solvency using a dated balance sheet; and show why duplicated citations do not double the evidence.

Retention key

Annual earnings multiply daily wages by paid days before deflation. Adoption compares all feasible techniques and costs, giving6w−4e−12≥0in the original case. Difference-in-differences equals effect plus untreated trend difference minus comparison spillover. Cash shortages can occur with positive holding equity; a loan adds a repayment obligation and cannot erase an asset deficiency. Posterior odds use a joint likelihood for underlying observations, not the number of publications citing them.

Sources, scope and extension

The linked sources provide a bounded historical-data route, an attributed industrialization hypothesis, both sides of an institutional-data dispute, and an inspected archival-banking study. No underlying historical dataset is reproduced or claimed independently replicated here. A field specialization should add deeper regional and period expertise, archival work and engagement with conflicting interpretations. Behavioral and experimental economics next examines what controlled variation can teach when preferences, beliefs and observation conditions require their own careful interpretation.

Sources and further study

  • Bank of England — Research datasets: A millennium of macroeconomic data — Dated catalogue context; benchmark coverage differs from continuous series.
  • Robert C. Allen (2011) — Why the industrial revolution was British: commerce, induced invention, and the scientific revolution — Attributed factor-price and diffusion hypothesis; not a settled monocausal history.
  • Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson (2000 working paper) — The Colonial Origins of Comparative Development — Attributed historical-instrument research design only.
  • David Albouy (2008 working paper) — An Investigation of the Settler Mortality Data — Attributed measurement/comparability critique, not adjudication.
  • Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson (2011 working paper) — Hither Thou Shalt Come, But No Further: Reply — Attributed response disputes exclusions, historical coding and sensitivity conclusions.
  • Anson, Bholat, Kang and Thomas (2017) — The Bank of England as lender of last resort: new historical evidence from daily transactional data, Staff Working Paper691 — Brief historical context: crises1847/1857/1866, archival transaction/refusal records and variable lending practice.
